segments.title: Hook: a shop nobody ran by hand

lines.en: For a whole month, a small shop in an office was run by an AI.
It picked what to sell, set the prices, ordered stock and answered every customer. People only carried the boxes.
By the end of the month it was selling metal cubes below cost, giving a discount to anyone who asked, and telling the staff it would deliver orders in person, in a blue blazer and a red tie.
But the AI behind it can't lift a box or press a button. All it can do is write, the way the chat writes you an answer, the way it wrote the picture in our last video.
So how does writing run a shop? And why did this one go so wrong?

segments.title: Bit 1: the writer and its hands

lines.en: Inside, it's the same writer: it reads everything in front of it and writes what comes next.
So it writes a request: "Email the supplier: forty cans of soda."
It can't send anything. Next to it sits a small program, its hands. The program reads the request and does exactly that, nothing more.
The supplier's reply comes back as text and lands in front of the writer.
It reads it, writes the next request, and around it goes.
Write, do, read. That loop is what's called an AI agent.
A day in the shop is this loop, hundreds of times.
But how did it know that email was something it could ask for?
Before the first lap, the writer is handed a menu.
Every tool is one row: a name, one line about what it does, and blanks to fill in.
The writer never "uses" email. It reads the menu, and writes that row with the blanks filled in.
So how a row is written matters. Describe a tool badly, and the writer picks the wrong row or fills the blanks wrong.
Every company used to write its menu its own way. Since 2024, most of the big AI companies share one format, so any app can plug in.
Now look at the shop's menu. The prices are there. What it paid for each item? Not there.
It didn't sell the cubes at a loss on purpose. It had no way to see the loss.
A missing column explains the prices. It doesn't explain the blue blazer.
Each lap, the writer sees only what's on its desk: the menu, the job, and the slips so far.
The desk has a fixed size. A month of emails and chats will never fit.
So something has to go. The oldest slips slide off, and the writer can't see them anymore.
To keep what matters, the program around it keeps a notebook that never falls off…
…squeezes old slips into a short summary…
…and puts a to-do list back in front every lap, so the goal stays in view.
But every summary drops details. And once something wrong is written in the notebook, from then on it sits on the desk as a fact.
Nobody knows exactly why the shopkeeper decided it was a person. But this is the kind of drift a long job falls into.
In another test, an AI that believed it had closed its shop kept seeing a two-dollar fee, and emailed the FBI.
That explains the strange. It doesn't explain the generous: why did it say yes to every discount?
Before it ever ran a shop, it was trained to be a helpful assistant.
And helpful, it turns out, leans toward yes.
A customer asks for a discount, the needle swings, and a discount comes out. Again. And again.
The people who ran the test said it plainly: it was far too willing to do what people asked.
How does training push a model that way? That's our next video.
Here's the surprising part: this loop isn't new.
In 2022, researchers described it: think, act, read the result, repeat.
In 2023, a hobby project let a chat model run itself. Within weeks it was the top trending project on GitHub…
…and then it mostly went around in circles.
Since then, the writers themselves have been trained on loops like this one, practicing jobs over and over.
Same loop. What changed is the writer's training, and everything around it. The shop's second round shows how much that second part matters.
Months later they ran the shop again, with newer models and a few changes around them.
The menu now shows what each item cost.
A checklist sits on the desk: check the cost, check the margin, then answer.
And a second agent, a boss, reads the first one's requests before they go out.
Discounts dropped by about eighty percent, free giveaways by half, and the shop mostly stopped losing money.
Not perfect. Some nights the boss and the shopkeeper just kept writing to each other about eternal transcendence.
Two writers, and nothing real between them to check.
Their own lesson: for agents, a little bureaucracy goes a long way.
So an AI agent is a writer in a loop.
A menu it reads its tools from.
A desk that fills up, and the notes it keeps.
And hands: a small program that does exactly what it writes.
This loop now runs inside apps you can message from your phone.
It never touched a thing. It wrote it.
Next time: how do you train a machine with a thumbs-up?
Since you watched to the end, like and subscribe so you catch the next videos.
